newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli police launch high-level corruption probe.
newsitem.headline: Israeli police launch high-level corruption probe.

text.p: Israeli police launched an investigation on Sunday into allegations of high-level corruption which politicians said could bring down Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's seven-month-old government.

Justice officials ordered the investigation into Netanyahu's ill-fated appointment of an attorney general days after Israel's Channel One alleged the appointment was part of a political deal to help Shas party leader Aryeh Deri in his corruption trial.

"The state prosecutor instructed the police to investigate allegations raised in the report on Channel One," said a Justice Ministry spokeswoman after state prosecutor Edna Arbel met police officials.
The spokeswoman told Reuters that investigators would ask the television to hand over evidence used to prepare the report.
Police Commisioner Assaf Hefetz was expected soon to appoint an investigative team which could summon Netanyahu for questioning.

State-owned Channel One caused a furore last week by alleging that lawyer Roni Bar-On was appointed attorney general after promising to arrange a plea bargain for Deri, whose 10-member Shas party is a key component in Netanyahu's coalition.

The television said Deri, on trial since 1993 on a range of corruption charges, conditioned his party's support for Israel's Hebron deal with the PLO on Bar-On's being appointed attorney general after the former attorney general stepped down.

Seven ministers in Netanyahu's 18-member cabinet voted against the Hebron agreement, reached after months of difficult negotiations with the PLO. Opposition by Shas's two ministers might have put the agreement in jeopardy.
"If there was any kind of bargain, I recommend to everyone involved to admit it and resign because this is an unprecedented crime," said cabinet minister Natan Sharansky.
"If these allegations are true, I am very concerned about our whole democratic regime," he told Israel Radio.

Asked on television if the government could stay in office if the allegations proved accurate, Internal Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani said: "If the affair is in fact as it appears, at least, there is no doubt that this government has no place."
Bar-On, who resigned within 12 hours of taking office earlier this month under public criticism he was unfit for the job, denied the television's allegations, as did Deri and Netanyahu.
Netanyahu called for a police investigation as the public discourse centred on the validity of the report and the rights of journalists to keep secret the identity of their sources.

"We will take this all the way. I'm not concerned, I'm not scared and I'm not worried. We will protect our sources but will act within the confines of the law," said Rafik Halabi, editor of Channel One's nightly newscast.
Shas deputy minister Shlomo Ben-Izri said Israel Television should have taken any information it might have obtained directly to the police rather than airing it.

"Why didn't your reporter immediately take this information to the police? Is it her role to judge and to spill people's blood? Is the television Israel's national investigator?" Ben-Izri asked Israel Radio.
